name: Tigrinya
confidence_why: Kogan 1997 and Bulakh & Kogan 2013 describe Tigrinya word stress as weak, non-phonological and overridden by phrase intonation, Leslau 1941's fieldwork and Buckley 1997 say the same, and the only placement rules to the contrary are nineteenth-century ones (Praetorius 1871, Schreiber 1887, De Vito 1895) that rest on other people's transcriptions and contradict one another, though Bulakh & Kogan 2013 admit the prosody has never been systematically studied.
catalog_citation: Kogan, Leonid E. 1997. Tigrinya. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 424-445. London: Routledge.
catalog_locator: p. 429, section 'Prosody' (chapter head '18 Tigrinya / Leonid E. Kogan' at p. 424)
catalog_quote: Stress in Tigrinya has no phonological value and easily shifts from one syllable to another. Dynamic stress is very weak and sometimes almost imperceptible. In many cases it falls on the last syllable, e.g. the euphonic -i: ra' asi 'head', sdbdyti 'woman', Pitch is an important element of the Tigrinya stress pattern, but it is also rather unstable. Dynamic stress and pitch may not coincide: ndbdrd 'to be' (" — high pitch; ~ — dynamic stress). Sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word, The relationship between these two features requires further investigation, but it is clear that rhythmical units very often do not coincide with single words.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had
sweep_summary: Tigrinya is not in the catalog. Of the two title-works with stress in the title, Walther 1999 (Deklarative prosodische Morphologie) is prosodic MORPHOLOGY (gemination, reduplication, coalescence, spirantization in Tigrinya verbs) with no stress/accent section — confirmed from the DNB table of contents. the full text is closed. Downing 2010 (Accent in African languages, Survey of Word Accentual Patterns, pp. 381-428, doi 10.1515/9783110198966.1.381) is a secondary continental survey that Glottolog links to Tigrinya; it is paywalled everywhere checked (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, GUP, BASE/CORE blocked) and StressTyp2 has no Tigrinya entry (0 of 699; No open first-hand stress source beyond those already held by the project from the the compilation was found; The best first-hand statement read is Kogan 1997: 429 (stress non-phonological, weak, mobile, mostly final; pitch and dynamic stress dissociate; sentence intonation dominant), corroborated by Leslau 1941 §26 (Akkele Guzay fieldwork: word accent barely perceptible, pre-geminate syllable more intense, final syllable also accented) and De Vito 1895 (mostly final), while Praetorius 1871 (penult, from Beke/Salt lists) and Schreiber 1887 (initial/antepenult) disagree; Bulakh & Kogan 2013: 267 state prosody has never been systematically studied.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tigrinya has no contrastive or fixed word stress: dynamic stress is weak, unstable and non-phonemic, with a tendency for prominence on the word-final syllable; pitch and dynamic stress can fall on different syllables, and phrase/sentence intonation overrides word-level prominence. Corroborated first-hand by Leslau 1941 §26 p. 15 (Akkele Guzay: 'L'accent du mot est très difficile à noter, car le mot n'a presque pas de relief dans la phrase et son accent s'efface devant l'accent de la phrase. Même dans un mot prononcé isolément le débit est uni.. une syllabe suivie d'une consonne géminée a plus d'intensité.. mais dans ces mots, comme d'ailleurs dans la plupart des mots, la dernière syllabe est également accentuée') and by Bulakh & Kogan 2013 §2.1.2 p. 267 ('Просодия Т.я. систематически не исследовалась.. динамическое ударение выражено слабо и акустически почти неуловимо. Фонологического значения ударение не имеет.' = 'The prosody of Tigrinya has not been systematically investigated.. dynamic stress is weakly expressed and acoustically almost imperceptible. Stress has no phonological value.').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Kogan 1997 or Leslau 1941. Only Praetorius 1871 §97 (from Salt's transcriptions) speaks of a 'Nebenaccent' on the final syllable of trisyllables with antepenult main accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Kogan: final-syllable prominence 'in many cases', notably on the euphonic -i; pitch peak and dynamic stress may sit on different syllables (näbärä). Leslau: syllables before a geminate carry extra intensity, final syllable also accented in most words. Nineteenth-century grammars (Praetorius 1871 penult/antepenult with heavy-final attraction; Schreiber 1887 initial in disyllables, antepenult in longer words; De Vito 1895 mostly final in disyllables) give mutually contradictory fixed rules, consistent with the modern 'weak, unstable, non-phonemic' classification.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement, explicitly subordinated to sentence intonation; Kogan notes rhythmical units often do not coincide with single words; Leslau says even citation forms are delivered evenly. Kogan's sketch is of standard (Eritrean/Tigray) Tigrinya generally; Leslau's data are Akkele Guzay (Eritrea).
new_statements.identity_note: Kogan 1997 and Bulakh & Kogan 2013 describe Tigrinya generally (tigr1271, standard Eritrean/Tigray usage). Leslau 1941 describes the Akkele Guzay dialect of Eritrea. Niguss 2021 (silent on stress) describes Rayya Tigrinya (southern Tigray). Praetorius 1871 is based on Aksum/Adwa plus Salt's 'Hauasa' list.

new_statements.reading: Tigrinya word stress is non-contrastive, weak and mobile, with a tendency toward the final syllable; pitch prominence and dynamic stress can dissociate, and phrase intonation overrides word-level stress. This is the standard modern reference statement and agrees with Leslau's 1941 first-hand fieldwork (weak word accent, extra intensity before geminates, final syllable also accented) and with De Vito 1895 (mostly final); the older penult/initial/antepenult rules of Praetorius 1871 and Schreiber 1887 rest on missionary or third-party transcriptions. Bulakh & Kogan 2013 add that the prosody has never been systematically studied and that pitch accent claims are unverified. A coding for this language should therefore be 'weak/non-phonological stress, predominantly final, mobile' with low confidence, or 'no fixed word stress'.

new_statements.quote: § 97 Bei der Untersuchung über die Betonung sind wir auf Bk. S. beschränkt, da L. den Tonfall nirgends bezeichnet. Zweisilbige Wörter haben den Ton in der Regel auf der Penultima ausgenommen wenn die letzte Silbe geschlossen ist und einen langen Vokal enthält [...] Im Dialekt von Hauasa hingegen wird die allgemeine Gültigkeit obiger Regel durch zahlreiche Ausnahmen beeinträchtigt indem die ultima mag sie consonantisch oder vokalisch auslauten oft den Ton hat [...] Bei dreisilbigen Wörtern ruht der Hauptton in der Regel auf der Antipenultima [...] auf die Ultima muss dann ein Nebenaccent fallen [...] Obige Beobachtungen über die Betonung können dem mangelhaften Material entsprechend nur als sehr unvollkommen gelten
new_statements.translation: § 97 For the investigation of stress we are restricted to Bk. [Beke] and S. [Seetzen], since L. [Lefebvre] nowhere marks the accent. Disyllabic words have the stress as a rule on the penult, except when the last syllable is closed and contains a long vowel [...] In the dialect of Hauasa, by contrast, the general validity of the above rule is impaired by numerous exceptions, in that the ultima, whether it ends in a consonant or a vowel, often carries the stress [...] In trisyllabic words the main stress rests as a rule on the antepenult [...] a secondary accent must then fall on the ultima [...] The above observations on stress, in keeping with the deficient material, can only count as very imperfect.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables: penult by default; final if the final syllable is closed and has a long vowel (probably also if closed by two consonants). Trisyllables: main stress on the antepenult with a secondary accent on the final; if the penult is long or closed it often (not always) takes the stress; a closed final with a long vowel pulls the stress rightwards in Beke's data. In Seetzen's 'Hauasa' glossary the ultima is often stressed regardless. Observations cover only unsuffixed nouns.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in trisyllables a Nebenaccent (secondary accent) falls on the ultima, which Seetzen usually marks explicitly (p. 138-139), and which lengthens a final -i (written -ih).
new_statements.exceptions: Penult rule exceptions listed as rare in Beke (melhäs, mebräk, nihib, sigäm..), numerous in Seetzen's Hauasa dialect (final stress); many deviations involve a guttural + a syllable; when a form CVCiC is followed by a stressed copula the accent retreats to the penult to avoid two adjacent stressed syllables; author calls the whole account very imperfect and based on defective material.
new_statements.identity_note: Praetorius 1871's stress remarks describe two 19th-century glossary varieties, not the Aksum/Adwa dialect of his texts: 'Bk.' = Beke's 'Tigre' glossary (southern Tigray, strongly Amharicised) and 'S.' = Seetzen's 1808 glossary of 'Hauasa' (scanned also 'Hanasa'/'Haoasa'; a trans-Takaze dialect he places near Walkayt), with the Hauasa data leaning toward final stress. Buckley's data come from Leslau 1941 (Akkele Guzay) and a native speaker consultant. The wrong item at the Bulakh 2023 link (Bulakh 2020, ALP) is on standard Tigrinya but says nothing about stress.

new_statements.quote: As Ullendorff [1955: 194] notes, "stress in Tigrinya falls almost invariably on the last syllable" (see also Leslau 1941: 15). The lack of a clear metrical stress system means that the third property which supports final extrasyllabicity in Arabic cannot be tested for Tigrinya; but certainly, stress placement provides no motivation for it in Tigrinya.

new_statements.quote: [p. 193] We thus find in Tna that sentence stress and rhythm are the predominant element to which the stress of individual words is subordinated. But in the case of the isolated word as well as in the sentence-context emphasis on the last syllable is clearly audible. [p. 194] While stress in Tna falls almost invariably on the last syllable, pitch moves with some freedom and is primarily conditioned by the sentence-context. The two rarely coincide. These findings reinforce my assertions about the stress conditions in the traditional pronunciation of Go'oz. Tna reflects the position in classical Ethiopic with some accuracy. Here, too, stress is non-phonemic.

new_statements.relation_note: Type differs from the catalog's classification: the catalog (Kogan 1997) codes Tigrinya as no-word-stress ('no phonological value.. easily shifts.. in many cases it falls on the last syllable'), whereas Ullendorff states a regular placement, stress 'almost invariably on the last syllable' in isolation and in context, while agreeing that it is non-phonemic, weak relative to sentence rhythm, and dissociated from pitch. It agrees with the on-file Buckley 1997 statement (fixed final; Buckley's fn. 12 quotes this very p. 194, now verified first-hand), with Leslau 1941 and De Vito 1895 (mostly final) as summarised held by the project, and against Praetorius 1871's penult/weight rule, which Ullend…
new_statements.rule_in_words: From his own fieldwork (five years in Eritrea/Ethiopia, fluent in Tigrinya) Ullendorff holds that Tigrinya word stress is expiratory but non-phonemic and falls almost invariably on the final syllable, audible both in isolated words and in connected speech; it is subordinated to sentence stress and rhythm; pitch is a separate parameter that moves freely with the sentence context and rarely coincides with stress (following Kolmodin 1910 on fixed word melodies). He endorses da Leonessa 1928 and Conti Rossini 1940 ('si fa cadere sempre sulla vocale.. dell'ultima sillaba': kälbí, nägärú) and Leslau 1941 ('dans la plupart des mots, la dernière syllabe est également accentuée'), and attributes Salt's and Beke's divergent older markings to confusion of pitch with stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described; word stress said to be subordinate to sentence rhythm, pitch independent of stress
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost invariably' final, no exceptions listed for Tigrinya; contrasts drawn with Tigre (weak, shifting stress, pitch and stress more often coalesce), Amharic (no strong expiratory stress; only in verbs some stability: penult in biliterals, antepenult in tri-/quadriliterals), Gurage and Harari (as Amharic).
new_statements.identity_note: Ullendorff's statements rest on his own 1940s fieldwork in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia (Preface: five-year stay, fluency in Tigrinya); no dialect is singled out, and he cites Conti Rossini's examples (kälbí 'dog', nägärú 'he said'). Kifle 2011 describes standard (Eritrean) Tigrinya, with examples from the newspaper Haddas Ertra; it has no phonology chapter.

readall_conflicts: Praetorius 1871 (§ 97, pp. 136-139) gives a weight-sensitive penult/antepenult rule (penult in disyllables unless the final syllable is closed with a long vowel; antepenult with a secondary accent on the final in trisyllables), which contradicts the catalog's existing statements from Kogan 1997 (stress has no phonological value, is weak and mobile, and mostly final) and the final-stress statement of Ullendorff 1955: 194 as quoted in Buckley 1997 fn. 12 ('falls almost invariably on the last syllable'). The conflict is old and already discounted in the existing statements: Praetorius' rule rests entirely on Beke's and Seetzen's early-19th-century glossary transcriptions (not on Praetorius' own hearing; Lefebvre's data mark no accent), he reports that Seetzen's 'Hauasa' dialect often stresses the ultima, and he closes by calling his observations 'sehr unvollkommen'. Buckley 1997 adds nothing contradictory: he accepts final stress from Ullendorff and stresses the 'lack of a clear metrical stress system'. Buckley 1994 and the mis-linked Bulakh 2020 ALP article are silent; Ullendorff 1955, Bulakh 2023 and Kifle 2012 could not be opened. Ullendorff 1955 (pp. 193-194, now read first-hand from the open DLI scan) says Tigrinya stress is non-phonemic but falls 'almost invariably on the last syllable', in isolation and in context, subordinate to sentence rhythm and independent of pitch; the catalog codes Tigrinya as no-word-stress after Kogan 1997 ('no phonological value and easily shif…

sources.quote: a) L'accent du mot est très difficile à noter, car le mot n'a presque pas de relief dans la phrase et son accent s'efface devant l'accent de la phrase. Même dans un mot prononcé isolément le débit est uni. b) Une règle générale qui semble se dégager est qu'une syllabe suivie d'une consonne géminée a plus d'intensité qu'une syllabe ayant une consonne simple : sällim « noir », qäddus « saint »; mais dans ces mots, comme d'ailleurs dans la plupart des mots, la dernière syllabe est également accentuée. c) L'informateur du dialecte décrit ici prononce avec gémination une consonne de la syllabe finale accentuée : sällim(m) « noir ».
sources.locator: § 26 Accent (p. 15 per prior index; scanned text, line-break hyphenation joined)
sources.note: §26 Accent (p. 15), Akkele Guzay dialect: word accent very hard to note, the word has almost no relief in the phrase and its accent yields to phrase accent; even in isolation delivery is even; a syllable followed by a geminate has more intensity, but in these as in most words the last syllable is also accented.

sources.citation: Schreiber, J. 1887. Manuel de la langue tigraï, parlée au centre et dans le nord de l'Abyssinie, vol. 1. Vienne: Hoelder.
sources.note: 'Accent' (pp. 10-11): affixes unaccented; disyllables regularly accented on the first syllable (unless it has a 6th-order/ə vowel and the second does not); words of 3+ syllables most often antepenult; later notes say accent is 'un peu incertain' in several forms.

sources.citation: Hellmuth, Sam & Mary Pearce. 2020. North Africa and the Middle East. In C. Gussenhoven & A. Chen (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody, ch. 12. Oxford: OUP (author accepted version 2019).
sources.note: Second-hand: Tigrinya stress described as shifting readily, dynamic correlates and pitch not always parallel; quotes Kogan 1997 that sentence intonation predominates over word stress (cites p. 439, but the passage is on p. 429 of the 1997 volume).

sources.citation: Hellmuth, Sam & Mary Pearce. 2019/2020. Prosodic typology of the languages of the Middle East and North Africa (ch. 12). In C. Gussenhoven & A. Chen (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody. Oxford: OUP.
sources.quote: The position of stress in Tigrinya has been described as shifting readily from one position to another and is not always marked in parallel by dynamic stress correlates (intensity/duration) and pitch. Kogan (1997: 439) suggests therefore that 'sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word', resembling descriptions noted above for Amazigh varieties which lack stress.
sources.note: Secondary; summarises Kogan 1997 only (the cited page 439 is a slip; the passage is on p. 429). Adds nothing first-hand.

sources.citation: Bulakh, M. S. & L. E. Kogan. 2013. Tigrin'ja jazyk. In M. S. Bulakh, L. E. Kogan & O. I. Romanova (eds.), Jazyki mira: Semitskie jazyki. Efiosemitskie jazyki, 260-310. Moskva: Academia.
sources.note: §2.1.2 (p. 267): prosody of Tigrinya has not been systematically studied; dynamic stress is weakly expressed and acoustically almost imperceptible, as in other living Ethiosemitic languages; stress has no phonological value; reports of musical (pitch) accent need verification.

sources.citation: Bulakh, Maria S. & Leonid E. Kogan. 2013. Tigrin'ja jazyk [The Tigrinya language]. In M. S. Bulakh, L. E. Kogan & O. I. Romanova (eds.), Jazyki mira: Semitskie jazyki. Efiosemitskie jazyki, 260-310. Moskva: Academia.
sources.quote: 2.1.2. Просодия Т.я. систематически не исследовалась. Принято считать, что, как и в других живых эфиосемитских языках, динамическое ударение выражено слабо и акустически почти неуловимо. Фонологического значения ударение не имеет. Встречающиеся в литературе указания на наличие в Т.я. музыкального ударения нуждаются в проверке.
sources.note: [EN] The prosody of Tigrinya has not been studied systematically. It is generally held that, as in the other living Ethio-Semitic languages, dynamic stress is weakly expressed and acoustically almost imperceptible. Stress has no phonological value. Claims in the literature of a pitch accent in Tigrinya need verification. — No placement rule given.

sources.citation: De Vito, Lodovico. 1895. Grammatica elementare della lingua tigrigna. Roma.
sources.quote: Nelle parole di due sillabe l'accento tonico cade per lo più sull'ultima, p. es. selèf; ma se questa ha la vocale e, e talvolta i, l'accento retrocede sulla prima, p. es. dènghez, kébdi. Nelle parole con tre o più sillabe, l'accento cade di solito sulla vocale di più chiara pronunzia, e a preferenza sull'ultima se questa abbia una à, una o, od una u, p. es. ymellàles, woridù. — Il posto dell'accento tonico è del resto quasi sempre determinato dalla forma della parola.
sources.note: pp. 10-11: in disyllables tonic accent mostly on the last syllable, retracting to the first if the last has e (sometimes i); in 3+ syllables on the 'clearest' vowel, preferably the last if it has a, o, u; position 'almost always determined by the form of the word' (contradicts Schreiber 1887).

sources.citation: Schreiber, J. 1887. Manuel de la langue tigraï, vol. 1. Vienne: Hölder.
sources.quote: 2° Les mots de deux syllabes ont régulièrement l'accent tonique sur la première, à moins que celle-ci ne soit formée par une lettre du sixième ordre et que la deuxième ne soit d'un autre ordre [...] 3° Les mots de trois syllabes et plus ont le plus souvent l'accent tonique sur l'antipénultième; ainsi gäbärä = il fit, egziabihêr = Dieu, etc.
sources.note: [EN] Affixed particles are unaccented; disyllables regularly stressed on the first syllable unless it has a sixth-order (ə) vowel and the second does not; words of three or more syllables mostly on the antepenult. Missionary grammar, contradicts Leslau/Kogan/De Vito on finality.

sources.citation: Praetorius, Franz. 1871. Grammatik der Tigriñasprache in Abessinien. Halle: Buchhandlung des Waisenhauses.
sources.quote: Bei der Untersuchung über die Betonung sind wir auf Bk. S. beschränkt, da L. den Tonfall nirgends bezeichnet. Zweisilbige Wörter haben den Ton in der Regel auf der Penultima ausgenommen wenn die letzte Silbe geschlossen ist und einen langen Vokal enthält [...] Im Dialekt von Hauasa hingegen wird die allgemeine Gültigkeit obiger Regel durch zahlreiche Ausnahmen beeinträchtigt indem die ultima mag sie consonantisch oder vokalisch auslauten oft den Ton hat [...] Obige Beobachtungen über die Betonung können dem mangelhaften Material entsprechend nur als sehr unvollkommen gelten; sie beziehen sich zunächst auch nur auf das einzelne Nomen ohne Suffixe.
sources.locator: III. Betonung, § 97 (pp. 136-139 per prior index; scanned lightly corrected)
sources.note: §97 'Betonung' (pp. 136-139), second-hand from Beke's and Salt's accent-marked wordlists: disyllables usually penult unless the final is closed with a long vowel; Hauasa (Salt) dialect often final; trisyllables usually antepenult with secondary accent on the final; author calls the observations 'sehr unvollkommen', isolated nouns only.

sources.note: Only the table of contents was obtainable (DNB). The Tigrinya chapter is a constraint-based computational treatment of verb morphology: gemination, reduplication-as-infixation, vowel coalescence, spirantization. No section on Betonung/Akzent/stress anywhere in the book; 'prosodisch' here means prosodic morphology (moras, syllable roles, geminates), not word stress.
